references.text: Jesus asked the same question just before in the parable of the mustard seed: "What is the kingdom of God like?" ([ref:Luk 13:18-19|Luke 13:18-19]). Verse 20 introduces the parable of yeast as a parallel to this.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses exactly the same parable about yeast and asks the same question about what the kingdom of God can be compared to ([ref:Matt 13:33|Matthew 13:33]).

In Matthew, Jesus introduces the parable of the mustard seed with a similar phrasing: "The kingdom of heaven is like..." ([ref:Matt 13:31|Matthew 13:31]), showing Jesus' repeated use of the parable form to describe the kingdom of God.
Also in Mark, Jesus uses the rhetorical question "What shall we compare the kingdom of God to?" ([ref:Mark 4:30|Mark 4:30]), the same type of introduction as in Luke 13:20.

Jesus uses the same rhetorical question form earlier in the Gospel of Luke: "To what then shall I compare this generation?" ([ref:Luk 7:31|Luke 7:31]). The verb ὁμοιώσω (I will compare) is used in a similar way.

The prophet Isaiah asks a similar rhetorical question: "To whom then will you compare God?" ([ref:Jes 40:18|Isaiah 40:18]). The question of what the divine can be compared to has roots in the Old Testament.

Again in Isaiah, the question is asked: "To whom will you compare me?" ([ref:Jes 46:5|Isaiah 46:5]). Jesus' question about what the kingdom of God can be compared to has a similar rhetorical structure to these OT texts about God's incomparability.
